notes: \cpara{Opens with the question people put to the author, what AIs will be like and do, and in the next line calls it a trick question.}

\cpara{Sets up the comparison in the next line. Humans share even molecular machines such as ATP synthase with plants and bacteria; the post explains this by the conservation of genes that many other genes depend on. ATP synthase is found ``in all known organisms'' (Wikipedia, ``Rotating locomotion in living systems'').}
\cpara{The thesis in its sharpest form, offered with ``might'': two AI designs could have less in common than a human and a petunia, which share machinery like ATP synthase.}

\cpara{The answer to the opening question, and it is hedged (``might''): nothing guarantees that AIs form a natural class. The post's own reason why humans form one is a shared architecture; whether AIs made by shared methods would also cluster, the post does not take up. Quintin Pope later raised this, against a spoken version of the same picture (2023): ``it's a bad idea to use `the size of mind space' as an intuition pump for `how similar are things from two different parts of mind space'.''}

\cpara{Introduces the diagram. It shows a sphere labelled ``Minds-in-general''; inside it a tall ellipse, ``Posthuman mindspace''; at the ellipse's base a smaller oval, ``Transhuman mindspace'', holding a dot, ``Human minds''. Three made-up kinds, ``Bipping AIs'', ``Freepy AIs'' and ``Gloopy AIs'', sit at scattered places. The sizes illustrate the claim; nothing in the post measures them.}

\cpara{Puts humans in a small dot, since a sexually reproducing species cannot vary much. The argument is in ``The Psychological Unity of Humankind,'' posted the day before and not in the book: ``In a sexually reproducing species, complex adaptations are necessarily universal.''}
\cpara{Describes the transhuman region: minds smarter than us that would ``in some sense'' still be people.}
\cpara{Describes the posthuman region: whatever a transhuman might grow into.}
\cpara{Describes the rest of the sphere: possible AIs too odd to count even as posthuman.}
\cpara{Asks where natural selection, which also designs things, belongs on the map.}
\cpara{Answers: the map sits inside a larger space of optimization processes, with the first natural selection at the bottom, below humans.}

\cpara{Asks whether some powerful optimizers would not count as minds, offers Hutter's AIXI with ``Arguably'', and defers the question. AIXI is a formal agent that cannot be computed, and it does not model itself as part of the environment it acts on (Wikipedia, ``AIXI''). I take that to be what ``can't even recognize itself in a mirror'' refers to.}

\cpara{States the moral: do not generalize over all of mind design space. The picture of a space of possible minds, in place of one line between minds and non-minds, has a precedent in Aaron Sloman's ``The structure of the space of possible minds'' (1984): ``Clearly there is not just one sort of mind.''}
\cpara{The post's one argument for the moral, a count. The count is right: there are about $2^{10^{12}+1}$ bit strings of at most a trillion bits.}
\cpara{Gives the mirror case: an existential claim has as many chances to be true.}
\cpara{Restates the moral as the conclusion of the count.}

\cpara{Names two sources of mistaken generalizations: imagining yourself in the mind's place, and imagining that a mind would reject its own code as you would. The second is the error described in ``Ghosts in the Machine,'' earlier in the book. The parenthesis concedes that the first method is right about one mind, your own.}
\cpara{States the existential side as the post's conclusion, hedged with ``almost''.}
\cpara{Draws the practical rule: explain what a mind does from its particular makeup, since another mind may do it differently.}
\cpara{Closes on the move of defining minds that behave differently as not minds, the error treated in ``Arguing `By Definition','' earlier in the book.}
